message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"8.6","text":"For this reason, Jesus is concealed from the Hebrews who have received Moses as teacher, while Moses is hidden from those who have trusted Jesus; for since the teaching through both is one, God accepts the person who has trusted either of them. But trusting a teacher is for the sake of doing the things spoken by God. That this is so, our Lord himself says: “I praise you, Father of heaven and earth, because you hid these things from wise elders and revealed them to nursing infants.” Thus God himself hid a teacher from some, since they already knew what must be done, but revealed one to others, since they did not know what they ought to do.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τῶν Ἰησοῦ πεπιστευκότων","chosen":"those who have trusted Jesus","rationale":"The perfect of πιστεύω with a personal object can denote placing trust in someone; “believed Jesus” is also possible."},{"source_quote":"ἐξομολογοῦμαί σοι","chosen":"I praise you","rationale":"In an address to God, ἐξομολογοῦμαι can express praise or thanksgiving rather than confession; “I give thanks to you” is a viable alternative."},{"source_quote":"σοφῶν πρεσβυτέρων","chosen":"wise elders","rationale":"Both terms are retained as printed rather than harmonized with a familiar form of the quotation."},{"source_quote":"ὡς προεγνωκόσιν","chosen":"since they already knew","rationale":"The context contrasts prior knowledge of what to do with ignorance; the more formally temporal “since they had known beforehand” remains possible."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"8.7","text":"Therefore, neither are the Hebrews condemned for not knowing Jesus, because of the one who hid him, provided that, while doing the things through Moses .... they do not hate the one they did not know; nor, in turn, are those from the nations who did not know Moses condemned because of the one who concealed him, provided that they too, while doing the things spoken through Jesus, do not hate the one they did not know. Nor do people gain any benefit by calling their teachers “lords” while not performing servants’ duties. For this reason, our Jesus said to someone who repeatedly called him Lord but did nothing that he commanded: “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I say?” For saying will not benefit anyone, but doing will. In every way, therefore, good works are needed. Yet if anyone should be deemed worthy to recognize both of them as proclaiming one teaching, that man has been counted rich in God, having understood the ancient things to be new with respect to time and the new things to be old.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὰ δὲ δούλων μὴ ποιεῖν","chosen":"not performing servants’ duties","rationale":"The substantival phrase means the things characteristic of servants. In accordance with the reader-facing wording policy, δούλων is rendered “servants,” but it can denote slaves or owned or bonded servants; the contrast with “lords” invokes their subordinate status, obligations, and possible ownership."},{"source_quote":"πυκνότερον","chosen":"repeatedly","rationale":"The comparative adverb can mean “more frequently” or, idiomatically, “rather frequently”; the context emphasizes repeated address."},{"source_quote":"ἐκ παντὸς οὖν τρόπου","chosen":"In every way, therefore","rationale":"The idiom stresses necessity by every consideration; “by all means” is an alternative."},{"source_quote":"τά τε ἀρχαῖα νέα τῷ χρόνῳ καὶ τὰ καινὰ παλαιὰ ὄντα","chosen":"the ancient things to be new with respect to time and the new things to be old","rationale":"The rendering preserves the printed paradox. τῷ χρόνῳ may alternatively be understood as “with time” or “in relation to time.”"}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"πράττοντες τὰ διὰ Μωϋσέως .... ὃν ἠγνόησαν μὴ μισήσωσιν","issue":"The supplied text contains a clearly printed four-dot gap after “the things through Moses.” Source content and meaning are missing at this point, and the missing wording and its precise syntactic contribution cannot be recovered without invention. The gap is therefore retained in the translation.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":true}]},{"reference":"8.8","text":"As Peter was saying these things, the crowds entered the place where he was, as though summoned by someone. When he saw the large crowd flowing gently in like the quiet current of a river, he said to Maroones, “Where around here do you have a place better able to hold the crowds?” When Maroones led him on to an outdoor place laid out as a garden, the crowds followed. Peter took his stand on the not very high pedestal of a statue and, immediately upon greeting the crowd according to a devout custom, knowing that many among the crowds present had for many years been tormented by demons and numerous afflictions, gnashing their teeth amid wailing and falling down in supplication, he rebuked them and ordered them to remain quiet. Then, after promising healing once he had delivered his discourse, he began to speak as follows:","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ὥσπερ ποταμοῦ ἥσυχον ῥεῦμα πράως προσρέοντα","chosen":"flowing gently in like the quiet current of a river","rationale":"The comparison presents the approaching crowd as a calm river current rather than as a violent rush."},{"source_quote":"Μαροόνῃ","chosen":"Maroones","rationale":"The name is transliterated from its dative form; the corresponding nominative is Μαροόνης."},{"source_quote":"τόπον ὕπαιθρον κεκηπευμένον","chosen":"an outdoor place laid out as a garden","rationale":"κεκηπευμένον describes a place cultivated or arranged as a garden; “a cultivated open-air place” is also possible."},{"source_quote":"βρύχοντάς τε μετὰ οἰμωγῆς","chosen":"gnashing their teeth amid wailing","rationale":"βρύχω commonly describes gnashing, though “roaring” or “growling” is lexically possible in this depiction."},{"source_quote":"μετὰ τὸ διαλεχθῆναι","chosen":"once he had delivered his discourse","rationale":"The passive-form verb is used in the deponent sense of speaking or discoursing; “after he had spoken” is a less specific alternative."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"8.9","text":"As I begin to deliver the discourse concerning reverence for God to people who know nothing at all and whose minds have been stained by the slanders of Simon, our opponent, I have thought it necessary first to deliver a discourse on why one must not blame God, who made everything. I begin nowhere else than from the very occasion that he himself providentially presented at the opportune moment, so that it may be known that with good reason many people have been held fast by many demons and overtaken by strange afflictions, in order that in this too God’s justice may become apparent; and so that those who blame him through ignorance, even now, after learning how they ought to think, may call themselves back from their former accusation by speaking well and doing good, offering ignorance—the cause of their wicked audacity—as grounds for pardon.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ὑπὸ τῶν τοῦ ἀντικειμένου ἡμῖν Σίμωνος διαβολῶν","chosen":"by the slanders of Simon, our opponent","rationale":"The genitive construction identifies Simon as the one opposing the speakers and as the source of the slanders."},{"source_quote":"ἀπ᾽ αὐτῆς τῆς κατὰ πρόνοιαν ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ εὐκαίρως ὑποβληθείσης προφάσεως","chosen":"from the very occasion that he himself providentially presented at the opportune moment","rationale":"πρόφασις here can denote an occasion or starting point, not necessarily a deceptive pretext; αὐτοῦ most naturally refers to God."},{"source_quote":"εὐλόγως","chosen":"with good reason","rationale":"The adverb asserts that the demonic and physical afflictions occurred on reasonable or justifiable grounds, rather than merely describing them as intelligible."},{"source_quote":"τοῦ προτέρου ἐγκλήματος ἑαυτοὺς ἀνακαλέσωνται","chosen":"may call themselves back from their former accusation","rationale":"The wording can depict withdrawal from their prior accusation against God. Alternatively, ἔγκλημα may denote the charge or culpability they incurred, yielding “extricate themselves from their former charge.”"},{"source_quote":"δι᾽ εὐφημίας τε καὶ εὐποιΐας","chosen":"by speaking well and doing good","rationale":"The rendering preserves the parallel between favorable speech and beneficial action; “through praise and good works” is also possible."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"8.10","text":"The matter is as follows: when the only good God had made everything well and handed it over to the human being who had come into being according to his image, the one who had come into being, breathing the divinity of the one who made him, being a true prophet and knowing all things, in honor of the father who had given him everything and for the salvation of the sons who came from him, as a genuine father preserving his goodwill toward the children brought into being by him, and wishing them, for their own benefit, to love God and be loved by him, revealed the road that leads to friendship with him. He taught by what human actions the sole God and Master of all rejoices; and, after declaring the things pleasing to him, he established an eternal law for all, one that cannot be burned up by war, is not secretly adulterated by any impious person, and is not hidden in a single place, but can be read by everyone. Consequently, through obedience to the law, everything was abundant for them: the finest fruits, the full span of years free from pain and disease, all securely bestowed along with every temperate condition of the air.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"παραδεδωκότος τῷ κατ᾽ εἰκόνα αὐτοῦ γενομένῳ ἀνθρώπῳ","chosen":"handed it over to the human being who had come into being according to his image","rationale":"παραδίδωμι here denotes handing over or entrusting the created order, while κατ᾽ εἰκόνα is retained as “according to his image.”"},{"source_quote":"τῆς τοῦ πεποιηκότος αὐτὸν πνέων θειότητος","chosen":"breathing the divinity of the one who made him","rationale":"The unusual genitive construction is preserved without resolving whether πνέων means breathing in, breathing forth, or manifesting the maker’s divinity."},{"source_quote":"τῶν ἐξ αὐτοῦ γενομένων υἱῶν","chosen":"the sons who came from him","rationale":"The phrase uses ἐξ αὐτοῦ to express origin from him."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς τοὺς ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ γενομένους παῖδας","chosen":"toward the children brought into being by him","rationale":"Unlike the preceding ἐξ αὐτοῦ, ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ marks agency, so the observable distinction is retained without implying that the phrases necessarily identify different groups."},{"source_quote":"τὴν πρὸς φιλίαν αὐτοῦ ἄγουσαν ἐξέφηνεν ὁδόν","chosen":"revealed the road that leads to friendship with him","rationale":"αὐτοῦ most naturally refers to God; “his friendship” is possible but less explicit about the direction of the road."},{"source_quote":"νόμον αἰώνιον ὥρισεν τοῖς ὅλοις","chosen":"he established an eternal law for all","rationale":"τοῖς ὅλοις may refer to all people or to the whole created order; the inclusive “for all” preserves that breadth."},{"source_quote":"μήτε πολέμῳ ἐμπρησθῆναι δυνάμενον μήθ᾽ ὑπὸ ἀσεβοῦς τινὸς ὑπονοθευόμενον μήτε ἐνὶ τόπῳ ἀποκεκρυμμένον, ἀλλὰ πᾶσιν ἀναγνωσθῆναι δυνάμενον","chosen":"one that cannot be burned up by war, is not secretly adulterated by any impious person, and is not hidden in a single place, but can be read by everyone","rationale":"The inability expressed by δυνάμενον is attached explicitly to being burned, while the next two participles describe separately negated states. The final δυνάμενον expressly states the law’s ability to be read by everyone."},{"source_quote":"ὑπὸ ἀσεβοῦς τινὸς ὑπονοθευόμενον","chosen":"is not secretly adulterated by any impious person","rationale":"ὑπονοθεύω denotes covert falsification, adulteration, or interpolation; “is not covertly tampered with” is a broader alternative."},{"source_quote":"τὰ τῶν ἐτῶν τέλεια καὶ ἄλυπα καὶ ἄνοσα","chosen":"the full span of years free from pain and disease","rationale":"The expression is elliptical; it can denote complete years or a full lifetime, characterized as painless and healthy."},{"source_quote":"μετὰ πάσης τῆς τῶν ἀέρων εὐκρασίας","chosen":"along with every temperate condition of the air","rationale":"εὐκρασία denotes a favorable balance or temperateness, while the plural ἀέρων can encompass atmospheric or climatic conditions."}],"source_issues":[]}]}
